Linked visualisations via Galois dependencies Journal: PACMPL Volume: 1 POPL 1 1
Roly Perera, Minh Nguyen, Tomas Petricek, Meng Wang

Abstract
. We present new language-based dynamic analysis techniques for linking visualisations and other structured outputs to data in a fine-grained way, allowing a user to interactively explore how data attributes map to visual or other output elements by selecting (focusing on) substructures of interest. This can help both programmers and end-users understand how data sources and complex outputs are related, which can be a challenge even for someone with expert knowledge of the problem domain. Our approach builds on bidirectional program slicing techiques based on Galois connections, which provide desirable round-tripping properties. Unlike the prior work in program slicing, our approach allows selections to be negated. In a setting with negation, the bidirectional analysis has a De Morgan dual, which can be used to link different outputs generated from the same input. This offers a principled language-based foundation for a popular interactive visualisation feature called brushing and linking where selections in one chart automatically select corresponding elements in another related chart. Although such view coordination features are valuable comprehension aids, they tend be to hard-coded into specific applications or libraries, or require programmer effort.



1

Extended paper with additional supporting material

1.
Introduction

Techniques for dynamic dependency analysis have been fruitful, with applications ranging from information-flow security
(
Sabelfeld and
Myers 2003
)
and optimisation
(
Kildall 1973
)
to debugging and program comprehension
(
Weiser 1981
;
De Lucia
et al. 1996
)
. There are, however, few methods suitable for fine-grained analysis of richly structured outputs, such as data visualisations and multidimensional arrays. Dataflow analyses
(
Reps
et al. 1995
)
tend to focus on analysing variables rather than parts of structured values. Where-provenance
(
Buneman
et al. 2001
)
and related data provenance techniques are fine-grained, but are specific to relational query languages. Taint tracking
(
Newsome and Song 2005
)
is also fine-grained, but works forwards from input to output. For many applications, it would be useful to be able to focus on a particular part of a structured output, and have an analysis isolate the input data pertinent only to that substructure.

This is a need that increasingly arises outside of traditional programming. Journalists and data scientists use programs to compute charts and other visual summaries from data, charts which must be interpreted by colleagues, policy makers and lay readers alike. Interpreting a chart correctly means understanding what the components of the visualisation actually
represent
, i.e. the mapping between data and visual elements. But this is a hard task, requiring time and expertise, even with access to the data and source code used to create the visualisation. In practice it is easy for innocent (but devastating) mistakes such as transposing two columns of data to go unnoticed
(
Miller 2006
)
. Since visualisations are simply cases of programs that transform structured inputs (data tables) into structured outputs (charts and other graphics), general-purpose language-based techiques for fine-grained dependency tracking should be able to help with this, by making it possible to reveal these relationships automatically to an interested user.

1.1.
Linking structured outputs to structured inputs

First, interpreting a chart would be much easier if the user were able to explore the relationship between the various parts of the chart and the underlying data interactively, discovering the relevant relationships on a need-to-know basis. For example, selecting a particular bar in a bar chart could highlight the relevant data in a table, perhaps showing only the relevant rows, as illustrated in Figure
1
. We could certainly do more and say something about the nature of the relationship (summation, in this case), but even just revealing the relevant data puts a reader in a much better position to fact-check or confirm their own understanding of what they are looking at. Indeed, visualisation designers sometimes create ‘‘data-linked’’ artefacts like these by hand, such as Nadieh Bremer’s award-winning visualisation of population density growth in Asian cities
(
Bremer and
Ranzijn 2015
)
, at the cost of significant programming effort. Libraries such as Altair
(
VanderPlas
et al. 2018
)
alleviate some of this work, but require data transformations to specified using a limited set of combinators provided (and understood) by the library.

Fine-grained linking of outputs to inputs, focusing on data for USA (left) and China (right).

What we would rather do instead is allow a data scientist to author analyses and visualisations using an expressive functional language like the one shown in Figure
1
, with data linking provided automatically for the computed artefact, as baked-in transparency feature. At the core of this is a program analysis problem: we want to be able to focus on a particular chart element, and determine the inputs that contribute to it. Given the output selection, this is a matter of performing some kind of backwards analysis to identify the relevant data. As well providing a path to automation, framing data linking as a program analysis problem invites interesting questions that a hand-crafted solution is unlikely to properly address. For example, does the union of two output selections depend on the union of their respective dependencies? Do dependencies ‘‘round-trip’’, in that they identify sufficient resources to reconstruct the selected output? Are they minimal? These questions are important to establishing trust and a language-based approach offers a chance to address them.

1.2.
Linking structured outputs to other structured outputs

Second, authors often present distinct but related aspects of data in separate charts. In this situation a reader should be able to focus on (select) a visual element in one chart or other structured output and automatically see elements of a different chart which were computed using related inputs. For example in Figure
2
below, selecting the bar on the left should automatically highlight all the related visual elements on the right. This is a well-recognised use case called
brushing and linking

(
Becker and
Cleveland 1987
)
, which is supported by geospatial applications like GeoDa
(
Anselin
et al. 2006
)
and charting libraries like Plotly, but tends to be baked into specific views, or require programmer effort and therefore anticipation in advance by the chart designer. Moreover these applications and libraries provide no direct access to the common data which explains why elements are related.

Figure 2
.
Linking visualisations via common data dependencies

Again, we would like to enable a more automated (and ubiquitous) version of brushing and linking, without imposing a burden on the programmer. They should be able to express visualisations and other data transformations using standard functional programming features such as those shown in Figure
2
, and have brushing and linking enabled automatically between computed artefacts which depend on common data. At the core of this requirement is a variant of our original program analysis problem: we want to select a part of the output and perform a backwards analysis to identify the required inputs, as before, but then also to perform a forwards analysis to identify dependent parts of the other output. Moreover, we would also like the brushing and linking feature to be able to provide a concise view of the data that explain why the two selections are linked. Note that the intuition behind the forwards analysis here is not the same as the one we appealed to in the context of round-tripping: there the (hypothetical) question was whether the selected data was
sufficient
to reconstruct the selected output, whereas to identify related items in another view, we must determine those parts for which the selected data is
necessary
. As before, a language-based approach offers the prospect of addressing these sorts of question in a robust way.

1.3.
Contributions

To make progress towards these challenges, we present a bidirectional analysis which tracks fine-grained data dependencies between input and output selections, with round-tripping properties characterised by Galois connections. Selections have a complement, which we use to adapt the analysis to compute fine-grained dependencies between two outputs which depend on common inputs. Recent program slicing techniques
(
Perera
et al. 2012
;
Perera
et al. 2013
;
Ricciotti et al. 2017
)
allow the user to focus on the output by ‘‘erasing’’ parts deemed to be irrelevant; the erased parts, called
holes
, are propagated backwards by a backwards analysis which identifies parts of the program and input which are no longer needed. Although these approaches also enjoy useful round-tripping properties characterised by Galois connections, they only allow focusing on
prefixes
of a structured output, rather than arbitrary substructures, a notion which is not closed under complement. Our specific contributions are as follows:

–

a new bidirectional dynamic dependency analysis which operates on selections of arbitrary parts of data values, for a core calculus with lists, records and mutual recursion, and a proof that the analysis is a Galois connection (§
3
);

–

a second bidirectional dependency analysis, derived from the first by De Morgan duality, which is also a Galois connection and which can be composed with the first analysis to link outputs to outputs, with an extended example based on matrix convolution (§
4
);

–

a richer surface language called Fluid, implemented in PureScript, with familiar functional programming features such as piecewise definitions and list comprehensions, and a further Galois connection linking selections between the core and surface languages (§
5
).

First we introduce the core calculus which provides the setting for the rest of the paper, and which will serve as the desugaring target for the surface syntax presented in §
5
.

2.
Core language

The core calculus is a mostly standard call-by-value functional language with datatypes and records. The main distinguishing feature is the use of
eliminators
, a trie-like pattern-matching construct that more familiar pattern-matching features like case expressions and piecewise function definitions easily desugar into. (A single core construct allows us to define the semantics of pattern-matching once and defer syntactic considerations to the surface language.) We give a big-step environment-based semantics, which is easier for the backward and forward dependency analyses in §
3
, and introduce a compact (term-like) representation of derivation trees in the operational semantics, called
traces
, which we will use to define the analyses over a fixed execution. Mutual recursion requires some care for the backwards analysis so we also treat that as a core language feature.

Syntax of core language

The terms of the language are defined in Figure
3
. These include Boolean constants

, integers
\displaystyle n
, variables
\displaystyle x
, and applications
\displaystyle{e}\,{e^{\prime}}
. Primitives are not first-class; the expression
\displaystyle{\phi}({\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern to a sequence of arguments. (First-class and infix primitives are provided by desugarings in §

and
\displaystyle{e}\,\textbf{{\text{{:}}}}\,{e^{\prime}}
, record construction

\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr

\displaystyle\hfil\displaystyle x{:}\;e\hfil

)
and record projection
\displaystyle{e}\textbf{{\text{{.}}}}{x}
. The final two term forms, anonymous functions
\displaystyle\uplambda{\sigma}
and recursive let-bindings
\displaystyle{\text{{let}}}\;{h}\;{\text{{in}}}\;{e}
where
\displaystyle h
is of the form

\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr

\displaystyle\hfil\displaystyle x{:}\;\sigma\hfil

, are explained below after we introduce the pattern-matching construct
\displaystyle\sigma
(
eliminator
). The typing rules for terms are given in Figure
4
, and are intended only to help a reader understand the language; therefore the rules are simple and do not include features such as polymorphism. The main typing rules of interest are the ones which involve eliminators.

2.2.
Eliminators

Eliminators
\displaystyle\sigma,\tau
are also defined in Figure
3
, and are inspired by
Connelly and
Morris 1995
’s notion of generalised trie
(
Connelly and
Morris 1995
)
, elaborated further by
Hinze 2000
. Eliminators specify how to match against a partial value of some type and select a continuation
\displaystyle\kappa
for further execution, where
\displaystyle\kappa
is either a term
\displaystyle e
or another eliminator
\displaystyle\sigma
. The Boolean eliminator
\displaystyle\{{\text{{true}}}{:}\;{\kappa},{\text{{false}}}{:}\;{\kappa^{\prime}}\}
selects either
\displaystyle\kappa
or
\displaystyle\kappa^{\prime}
depending on whether a Boolean value is
true
or
false
. The record eliminator
\displaystyle\{{\text{{(}}}\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\displaystyle\hfil\displaystyle x\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern matches a record with fields

\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr

\displaystyle\hfil\displaystyle x\hfil

and then returns
\displaystyle\kappa
with the variables

\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr

\displaystyle\hfil\displaystyle x\hfil

bound to the components of the record. The list eliminator
\displaystyle\{{\text{{[]}}}{:}\;{\kappa},(\textbf{{\text{{:}}}}){:}\;{\sigma}\}
maps the empty list to
\displaystyle\kappa
and a non-empty list to another eliminator
\displaystyle\sigma
which specifies how the head and tail of the list are to be matched. The variable eliminator
\displaystyle{x}{:}\;{\kappa}
extends the usual notion of trie, matching any value, binding it to
\displaystyle x
, and then returning
\displaystyle\kappa
. Eliminators resemble the ‘‘case trees’’ commonly used as an intermediate form when compiling languages with pattern-matching
(
Graf
et al. 2020
)
, and can serve as an elaboration target for more advanced features such as the piecewise definitions described in §
5
.

Typing rules for core language

The use of nested eliminators to match sub-values will become clearer if we consider the typing judgement
\displaystyle\Gamma\vdash\sigma:{A}\rightarrow{B}
for eliminators given in Figure
4
. (Eliminators always have function type, so this should be read as a four-place relation, with
\displaystyle\to
part of the notation.) The typing rule for variable eliminators reveals the connection between eliminators and functions: it converts a continuation
\displaystyle\kappa
which can be assigned type
\displaystyle B
under the assumption that
\displaystyle x
is of type
\displaystyle A
into an eliminator of type
\displaystyle{A}\rightarrow{B}
. The typing rule for Boolean eliminators says that to make an eliminator of type
\displaystyle{{\text{{Bool}}}}\rightarrow{A}
, we simply need two continuations
\displaystyle\kappa
and
\displaystyle\kappa^{\prime}
of type
\displaystyle A
. The rule for the empty record states that to make an eliminator of type
\displaystyle{{\text{{Rec}}}\;{{\text{{(}}}{\text{{)}}}}}\rightarrow{A}
, we simply need a continuation
\displaystyle\kappa
of type
\displaystyle A
. The rule for non-empty records allows us to treat an eliminator of type
\displaystyle{{\text{{Rec}}}\;{{\text{{(}}}\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\displaystyle\hfil\displaystyle x{:}\;A\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\displaystyle\hfil\textstyle x{:}\;A\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern as an eliminator of type

, representing the isomorphism between
\displaystyle{{A}\rightarrow{B}}\rightarrow{C}
and
\displaystyle{{A}\times{B}}\rightarrow{C}
but at the level of record types
(
Hinze 2000
)
. (Formalising eliminators precisely requires
Bird and Meertens 1998
-style nested datatypes
(
Bird and Meertens 1998
)
and polymorphic recursion, but these details need not concern us here.)

The typing rule for list eliminators
\displaystyle\{{\text{{[]}}}{:}\;{\kappa},(\textbf{{\text{{:}}}}){:}\;{\sigma}\}
combines some of the flavour of record and Boolean eliminators. To make an eliminator of type
\displaystyle{{\text{{List}}}\;{A}}\rightarrow{B}
, we need a continuation of type
\displaystyle B
for the empty case, and in the non-empty case, an eliminator of type
\displaystyle{A}\rightarrow{{{\text{{List}}}\;{A}}\rightarrow{B}}
which can be treated as an eliminator of type
\displaystyle{{A}\times{{\text{{List}}}\;{A}}}\rightarrow{B}
in order to process the head and tail.

2.2.1.
Eliminators as functions

We can now revisit the term forms
\displaystyle\uplambda{\sigma}
and
\displaystyle{\text{{let}}}\;{h}\;{\text{{in}}}\;{e}
. If
\displaystyle\sigma
is an eliminator of type
\displaystyle{A}\rightarrow{B}
, then
\displaystyle\uplambda{\sigma}
is an anonymous function of the same type. If
\displaystyle h
is of the form

\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr

\displaystyle\hfil\displaystyle x{:}\;\sigma\hfil

, then
\displaystyle{\text{{let}}}\;{h}\;{\text{{in}}}\;{e}
introduces a sequence of mutually recursive functions which are in scope in
\displaystyle e
. The typing rule for
\displaystyle{\text{{let}}}\;{h}\;{\text{{in}}}\;{e}
uses an auxiliary typing judgement
\displaystyle\Gamma\vdash h:\Delta
which assigns to every
\displaystyle x
in
\displaystyle\Delta
a function type
\displaystyle{A}\rightarrow{B}
as long as the
\displaystyle\sigma
to which
\displaystyle x
is bound in
\displaystyle h
has that type.

2.2.2.
Values

Values
\displaystyle v,u
, and environments
\displaystyle\rho
are also defined in Figure
3
, and are standard for call-by-value. (Environments are more convenient than substitution for tracking variable usage.) To support mutual recursion, the closure form
\displaystyle{\text{{cl}}}({\rho},{h},{\sigma})
captures the (possibly empty) sequence
\displaystyle h
of functions with which the function was mutually defined, in addition to the ambient environment
\displaystyle\rho
. For the typing judgements
\displaystyle\vdash\rho:\Gamma
and
\displaystyle\vdash v:A
for environments and values (Figure
4
), only the closure case is worth noting, which delegates to the typing rules for recursive definitions and eliminators.

2.2.3.
Evaluation

Figure
6
gives the operational semantics of the core language. In §
3
we will define forward and backward analyses over a single execution; in anticipation of that use case, we treat the operational semantics as an inductive data type, following the ‘‘proved transitions’’ approach of
Boudol and
Castellani 1989
for reversible CCS
(
Boudol and
Castellani 1989
)
. The inhabitants of this data type are derivation trees explaining how a result was computed, and the analyses will be defined by structural recursion over these trees. Expressed in terms of inference rules, these trees can become quite cumbersome, so we introduce an equivalent but more term-like syntax for them, called a
trace
(Figure
5
), similar to the approach taken by
Perera
et al. 2016
for
\displaystyle\pi
-calculus
(
Perera
et al. 2016
)
.

Figure 6
.
Operational semantics

The judgement
\displaystyle T::\rho,e\Rightarrow v
defined at the top of Figure
6
states that term
\displaystyle e
under environment
\displaystyle\rho
evaluates to value
\displaystyle v
, and that
\displaystyle T
is a proof term that witness that fact. (In the figure the traces appear in grey, to reinforce the idea that they are not part of the definition of
\displaystyle\Rightarrow
but rather a notation for its inhabitants.) The rules for Booleans, integers and lists are standard and have unsurprising trace forms. For variables, we give an explicit inductive definition of the environment lookup relation
\displaystyle\in
at the bottom of the figure, again so that later we can perform analysis over a proof that an environment contains a binding. The lambda rule is standard except that we specify
\displaystyle\varepsilon
for the sequence of definitions being simultaneously defined, since a lambda is not recursive. For record construction, the trace form contains a subtrace
\displaystyle T_{i}
for each field, and for record projection, which also uses the lookup relation
\displaystyle\in
, the trace form
\displaystyle{T_{\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\displaystyle\hfil\displaystyle x{:}\;v\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\displaystyle\hfil\textstyle x{:}\;v\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern The rule for (mutually) recursive functions
\displaystyle{\text{{let}}}\;{h}\;{\text{{in}}}\;{e}

\displaystyle h

\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr

\displaystyle\hfil\displaystyle x{:}\;\sigma\hfil

of function definitions, makes use of the auxiliary relation
\displaystyle\rho,h\twoheadrightarrow\rho^{\prime}
at the bottom of Figure

which turns
\displaystyle h
into an environment
\displaystyle\rho^{\prime}
binding each function name
\displaystyle x_{i}
to a closure
\displaystyle{\text{{cl}}}({\rho},{h},{\sigma_{i}})
capturing
\displaystyle\rho
and a copy of
\displaystyle h
. For primitive applications, the trace records the values of the arguments which were passed to the operation
\displaystyle\phi
. The rule for application
\displaystyle{e}\,{e^{\prime}}
is slightly non-standard, because it must deal with both mutual recursion and pattern-matching. First we unpack the recursive definitions
\displaystyle h
from the closure
\displaystyle{\text{{cl}}}({\rho_{1}},{h},{\sigma})
computed by
\displaystyle e

\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow

\displaystyle\rho_{2}
of closures. We then use the relation
\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow
explained below to match
\displaystyle v
against the eliminator
\displaystyle\sigma
, obtaining the branch
\displaystyle e^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu}
of the function to be executed and parameter bindings
\displaystyle\rho_{3}
. In addition to subtraces
\displaystyle T
and
\displaystyle U
for the function and argument, the application trace
\displaystyle{T}\,{U}\mathrel{\blacktriangleright}{w{:}\;T^{\prime}}
also has subtraces
\displaystyle w
for the pattern-match and
\displaystyle T^{\prime}
for the selected branch.

2.2.4.
Pattern matching

The judgement
\displaystyle w::v,\sigma\rightsquigarrow\rho,\kappa
also defined in Figure
6
states that eliminator
\displaystyle\sigma
can match
\displaystyle v
and produce environment
\displaystyle\rho
and continuation
\displaystyle\kappa
, with
\displaystyle\rho
containing the variable bindings that arose during the match.
Matches

\displaystyle w
are a compact notation for proof terms for the
\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow
relation, analogous to traces for the
\displaystyle\Rightarrow
relation, and again appear in grey in the figure.

Variable eliminators
\displaystyle{x}{:}\;{\kappa}
match any value, returning the singleton environment
\displaystyle x{:}\;v
and continuation
\displaystyle\kappa
. Boolean eliminators match any Boolean value, returning the appropriate branch and empty environment
\displaystyle\varepsilon
. List eliminators
\displaystyle\{{\text{{[]}}}{:}\;{\kappa},(\textbf{{\text{{:}}}}){:}\;{\sigma}\}
match any list. The nil case is analogous to the handling of Booleans; the cons case depends on the fact that the nested eliminator
\displaystyle\sigma
for the cons branch has the curried type
\displaystyle{A}\rightarrow{{{\text{{List}}}\;{A}}\rightarrow{B}}
. First, we recursively match the head
\displaystyle v
of type
\displaystyle A
using
\displaystyle\sigma
, obtaining bindings
\displaystyle\rho
and eliminator
\displaystyle\tau:{{\text{{List}}}\;{A}}\rightarrow{B}
as the continuation. Then the tail
\displaystyle v^{\prime}
is matched using
\displaystyle\tau
to yield additional bindings
\displaystyle\rho^{\prime}
and final continuation
\displaystyle\kappa^{\prime}
. Record matching is similar: the empty record case resembles the nil case, and the non-empty case relies on the nested eliminator having curried type
\displaystyle{{\text{{Rec}}}\;{{\text{{(}}}\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 3.
A bidirectional dynamic dependency analysis

We now extend the core language from §
2
with a bidirectional mechanism for tracking data dependencies. §
3.1
establishes a way of selecting (parts of) values, such as the height of a bar in a bar chart. §
3.2
defines a forward analysis function
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
which specifies how selections on programs and environments (collectively:
input selections
) becomes selection on outputs; selections represent
availability
, with the computed output selection indicating the data available to the downstream computation. §
3.3
defines a backward dependency function
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
specifying how output selections are mapped back to inputs; then selections represent demands, with the computed input selection identifying the data needed from the upstream computation. Both functions are monotonic; this will become important in §
3.4
, where show that
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
and
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
form a Galois connection, establishing the round-tripping properties sketched intuitively in §
1.1
which are important for trusting the results of the analyses.

3.1.
Lattices of selections

Our approach to representing selections is shown in Figure
7
. The basic idea is to parameterise the type
Val
of values by a (bounded) lattice
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}
of
selection states

\displaystyle\alpha
. We add selection states to Booleans, integers, records and lists. For our present purposes, we are only interested in dependencies between first-order data, so closures are not (directly) selectable, although they have selectable parts; closures also capture the
ambient availability
(explained in §
3.2.2
below), which is also a selection state
\displaystyle\alpha
. We parameterise the type
Term
of terms in the same way, but only add selection states to the term constructors corresponding to selectable values, allowing us to trace data dependencies back to expressions that appear in the source code. We return to this in §
5
.

and
\displaystyle\bot

Partial order on values

3.1.1.
Selections of a value

The analyses which follow will be defined with respect to a fixed computation, and so we will often need to talk about the selections of a given value. To make this notion precise, consider that the raw (unselectable) syntax described in §
2
can be recovered from a selectable term via an erasure operation
\displaystyle\lfloor v\rfloor:\textup{{Val}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Val}}\,{1}
which forgets the selection information, where
\displaystyle 1
is the trivial one-point lattice. We refer to
\displaystyle\lfloor v\rfloor
as the
shape
of
\displaystyle v
. Allowing
\displaystyle\bm{u},\bm{v}
from now on to range over raw values, and reserving
\displaystyle u,v
for selectable values, we can then define:

Definition 3.1 (Selections of
\displaystyle\bm{v}
).

Define
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
to be the set of all values
\displaystyle v\in\textup{{Val}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
with shape
\displaystyle\bm{v}
, i.e.
that erase to
\displaystyle\bm{v}
.

Since its elements have a fixed shape,
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}
is a ‘‘representable’’ functor: it is isomorphic to a function space whose domain is the set of selection positions in
\displaystyle\bm{v}
. In particular, the pointwise comparison of any
\displaystyle v,v^{\prime}
in
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
using the partial order
\displaystyle\sqsubseteq
of
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}
is well defined, as is the pointwise application (zip) of a binary operation
(
Gibbons 2017
)
. It should be clear that if
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}
is a lattice, then
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
is also a lattice, with
\displaystyle\top_{\bm{v}}
,
\displaystyle\bot_{\bm{v}}
,
\displaystyle\sqcap_{\bm{v}}
, and
\displaystyle\sqcup_{\bm{v}}
defined pointwise. For example, if
\displaystyle u
and
\displaystyle u^{\prime}
have the same shape and
\displaystyle v
and
\displaystyle v^{\prime}
have the same shape, the join of the lists
\displaystyle({u}\,\textbf{{\text{{:}}}}_{\hskip-0.49002pt\alpha}\,{v})
and
\displaystyle({u^{\prime}}\,\textbf{{\text{{:}}}}_{\hskip-0.49002pt\alpha^{\prime}}\,{v^{\prime}})
is defined and equal to
\displaystyle{(u\sqcup u^{\prime})}\,\textbf{{\text{{:}}}}_{\hskip-0.49002pt\alpha\sqcup\alpha^{\prime}}\,{(v\sqcup v^{\prime})}
. Similarly, the top element of
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
is the selection of
\displaystyle\bm{v}
which has
\displaystyle\top
at every selection position. (We omit the
\displaystyle\bm{v}
indices from the lattice operations if it is clear which lattice is being referred to.) The notion of the ‘‘selections’’ of
\displaystyle\bm{v}
extends to the other syntactic forms.

3.1.2.
Environment selections and hole equivalence

The notion of a ‘‘selection’’ of
\displaystyle\bm{v}
also extends pointwise to environments, so that
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
means the set of selectable environments
\displaystyle\rho^{\prime}
of shape
\displaystyle\bm{\rho}
, where the variables in
\displaystyle\rho^{\prime}
are bound to selections of the corresponding variables in
\displaystyle\bm{\rho}
. One challenge arises from the pointwise use of
\displaystyle\sqcup
to combine environment selections. Since environments contain other environments recursively through closures, environment join is a very expensive operation if treated naively. One implementation option is to employ an efficient representation of values which are fully unselected, which is the case for the majority of bindings in an environment.

We therefore enrich the set of selectable values
\displaystyle\textup{{Val}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
with a distinguished element
hole
, written
\displaystyle\square
, which is an alternative notation for
\displaystyle\bot_{\bm{v}}
for any
\displaystyle\bm{v}
, i.e. the selectable value of shape
\displaystyle\bm{v}
which has
\displaystyle\bot
at every selection position. The equivalence of
\displaystyle\square
to any such bottom element is established explicitly by the partial order defined in Figure
8
: the first rule always allows
\displaystyle\square
on the left-hand side of
\displaystyle\sqsubseteq
, and other rules allow
\displaystyle\square
on the right-hand side of
\displaystyle\sqsubseteq
as long as all the selections that appear on the left-hand side are
\displaystyle\bot
. (The rules for recursive definitions
\displaystyle h
, eliminators
\displaystyle\sigma
and terms
\displaystyle e
are analogous and are omitted.) If we write
\displaystyle\doteq
for the equivalence relation induced by
\displaystyle\sqsubseteq
on selectable values, which we call
hole-equivalence
, it should be clear that
\displaystyle\square\sqcup v\doteq v
and
\displaystyle\square\sqcap v\doteq\square
. This means the join of two selections
\displaystyle v,v^{\prime}
of
\displaystyle\bm{v}
can be implemented efficiently, whenever one selection is
\displaystyle\square
, by simply discarding
\displaystyle\square
and returning the other selection without further processing.

Definition 3.2 (Hole equivalence).

Define
\displaystyle\doteq
as the intersection of
\displaystyle\sqsubseteq
and
\displaystyle\sqsupseteq
.

Because
\displaystyle\square
is equivalent to
\displaystyle\bot_{\bm{v}}
for any
\displaystyle\bm{v}
, all such bottom elements are hole-equivalent. For example, the selectable value
\displaystyle{\square}\,\textbf{{\text{{:}}}}_{\hskip-0.49002pt\top}\,{\square}
is hole-equivalent to
\displaystyle{5_{\bot}}\,\textbf{{\text{{:}}}}_{\hskip-0.49002pt\top}\,{\square}
, but also to
\displaystyle{6_{\bot}}\,\textbf{{\text{{:}}}}_{\hskip-0.49002pt\top}\,{{{\text{{[]}}}_{\bot}}}
, and so the last two selections, even though they have different shapes, are hole-equivalent by transitivity. In practice we only use the hole ordering to compare selections with the same shape.

3.2.
Forward data dependency

We now define the core bidirectional data dependency analyses for a fixed computation
\displaystyle T::\bm{\rho},\bm{e}\Rightarrow\bm{v}
, where
\displaystyle T
is a trace. In practise one would first evaluate a program to obtain its trace
\displaystyle T
, and then run multiple forward or backward analyses over
\displaystyle T
with appropriate lattices. We start with the forward dependency function
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
which ‘‘replays’’ evaluation, turing input availability into output availability, with
\displaystyle T
guiding the analysis whenever holes in the input selection would mean the analysis would otherwise get stuck.
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
uses the auxiliary function
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptw}}}
for forward-analysing a pattern-match, which introduces the key idea of a selection as the data available to a downstream computation.

\displaystyle v,\sigma\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-1.60995ptw}}\rho,\kappa,\alpha

\displaystyle v
and
\displaystyle\sigma
forward-match along
\displaystyle w
to
\displaystyle\rho
and
\displaystyle\kappa
, with ambient availability
\displaystyle\alpha

3.2.1.
Forward match

Figure
9
defines a family of
forward-match
functions
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptw}}}
of type
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v},\bm{\sigma}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho},\bm{\kappa}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\times\mathcal{A}
for any
\displaystyle w::\bm{v},\bm{\sigma}\rightsquigarrow\bm{\rho},\bm{\kappa}
. (The definition is presented in a relational style for readability, but should be understood as a total function defined by structural recursion on
\displaystyle w
, which appears in grey to emphasise the connection to Figure
6
.) Forward-match replays the match witnessed by
\displaystyle w
, transferring the selections on the relevant parts of
\displaystyle v\in\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
to the output environment
\displaystyle\rho\in\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
, and from the relevant part of
\displaystyle\sigma\in\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\sigma}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
to the chosen continuation
\displaystyle\kappa\in\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\kappa}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
.

\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptw}}}
also returns the
meet
of the selection states associated with the part of
\displaystyle v
consumed by
\displaystyle\sigma
, which we call the
availability
of
\displaystyle v
(in the context of
\displaystyle\sigma
), since it represents the extent to which the demand implied by
\displaystyle\sigma
was met. A variable match consumes nothing of
\displaystyle v
and so the availability is simply
\displaystyle\top
, the unit for meet. A Boolean match consumes either
\displaystyle{\text{{true}}}_{\alpha}
or
\displaystyle{\text{{false}}}_{\alpha}
, with availability
\displaystyle\alpha
; empty list and record matches are similar. When we match a cons, we return the meet of the
\displaystyle\alpha
on the cons node itself with the availabilities
\displaystyle\beta
and
\displaystyle\beta^{\prime}
computed for
\displaystyle v
and
\displaystyle v^{\prime}
. Non-empty records are similar, but to process the initial part of the record, we supply the neutral selection state
\displaystyle\top
on the subrecord in order to use the definition recursively. (Subrecords are not first-class, but exist only as intermediate artefacts of the interpreter.)

One might imagine dispensing with the need for
\displaystyle w
by simply defining
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptw}}}
by case analysis on
\displaystyle v
and
\displaystyle\sigma
. However, it is then unclear how to proceed in the event that
\displaystyle v
is a hole. It would be legitimate to produce
\displaystyle\square
as the output continuation and
\displaystyle\bot
as the output selection state, but for the output environment to be well-typed, it must provide variable bindings corresponding to those introduced in the baseline computation where
\displaystyle\bm{v}
was matched against
\displaystyle\bm{\sigma}
. If
\displaystyle\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}
is defined with respect to a known
\displaystyle w
, this can be achieved via an additional rule
\displaystyle\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}
-hole-1
that defines the behaviour at hole to be the same as the behaviour at any
\displaystyle\doteq
-equivalent value in
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
. The
\displaystyle\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}
-hole-2
rule makes a similar provision for
\displaystyle\sigma
, which may also be a hole. Operationally, these rules can be interpreted as ‘‘expanding’’ enough of the holes in
\displaystyle v
or
\displaystyle\sigma
to make another rule of the definition match. There will be exactly one non-hole rule that matches, corresponding to the execution path originally taken, and although there may be multiple such expansions, the following property implies that the result of
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptw}}}
will be unique up to
\displaystyle\doteq
.

Lemma 3.3 (Monotonicity of
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptw}}}
).

Suppose
\displaystyle w::\bm{v},\bm{\sigma}\rightsquigarrow\bm{\rho},\bm{\kappa}
, with
\displaystyle v,\sigma\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptw}}\rho,\kappa,\alpha
and
\displaystyle v^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime}\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptw}}\rho^{\prime},\kappa^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}
. If
\displaystyle(v,\sigma)\sqsubseteq(v^{\prime},\sigma)
then
\displaystyle(\rho,\kappa,\alpha)\sqsubseteq(\rho^{\prime},\kappa^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime})
.

3.2.2.
Forward evaluation

Figure
9
also defines a family of
forward-evaluation
functions
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
of type
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho},\bm{e}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
for any
\displaystyle T::\bm{\rho},\bm{e}\Rightarrow\bm{v}
. Like forward-match, forward-evaluation is presented in a relational style, but should be understood as a total function defined by structural recursion on
\displaystyle T
. Forward evaluation replays
\displaystyle T
, using the input selection
\displaystyle(\rho,e)\in\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho},\bm{e}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
to determine an output selection
\displaystyle v\in\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
. The rules mirror those of the evaluation relation
\displaystyle\Rightarrow
, although there is an additional selection state input
\displaystyle\alpha
called the
ambient availability
. We explain this with reference to the application rule, which is the only point where a new ambient availability is assigned.

Function application

The rule assumes the application
\displaystyle{e}\,{e^{\prime}}
already has an ambient availability
\displaystyle\alpha
; at the outermost level this will usually be
\displaystyle\top
. The rule passes
\displaystyle\alpha
down when recursively forward-evaluating
\displaystyle e
and
\displaystyle e^{\prime}
, but computes a new selection state
\displaystyle\beta\sqcap\beta^{\prime}
when transferring control to the function, combining ambient availability
\displaystyle\beta
captured by the closure and
\displaystyle\beta^{\prime}
obtained by forward-matching the argument
\displaystyle v
with the eliminator
\displaystyle\sigma
of the closure, representing the availability of those parts of
\displaystyle v
demanded by the function. The ambient availability is used to upper-bound the availability of any selectable values constructed in the dynamic context of that function, establishing a dependency between the resources consumed by functions and resources they produce. The auxiliary function
\displaystyle\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998pt\rho,h}}:\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho},\bm{h}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho}^{\prime}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
for any
\displaystyle\smash{\bm{\rho},\bm{h}\twoheadrightarrow\bm{\rho^{\prime}}}
is given at the bottom of Figure
9
and follows
\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow
, but captures the ambient availability into each closure.

Other rules

All other rules pass the ambient availability into any subcomputations unchanged. Variable lookup disregards the ambient
\displaystyle\alpha
, simply preserving the selection on the returned value. The lambda rule captures it in the closure, along with the environment; the letrec rule passes it on to
\displaystyle\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}
so it is captured by recursive closures as well. Record projection is more interesting, disregarding not only the ambient
\displaystyle\alpha
but also the availability
\displaystyle\beta
of the record itself. Containers are considered to be independent of the values they contain: here,
\displaystyle v_{i}
has its own internal availability which is preserved by projection, but there is no implied dependency of the field on the record from which it was projected. Record construction also reflects this principle, preserving the field selections into the resulting record selection unchanged. But it also sets the availability of the record value to be the meet of
\displaystyle\alpha
and
\displaystyle\alpha^{\prime}
, reflecting the dependency of the container on the constructing expression and also on any resources consumed by the ambient function. The rules for nil, cons and integers are similar.

Hole case

A hole rule is also needed, because if
\displaystyle e
is
\displaystyle\square
, forward evaluation must continue; in particular, subsequent steps may extract non-
\displaystyle\square
values from
\displaystyle\rho
and result in non-
\displaystyle\square
outputs. The rule is similar to the rules for
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptw}}}
and again can be understood operationally as using the information in
\displaystyle T
to expand
\displaystyle\square
sufficiently for another rule to apply, with a result which is unique up to
\displaystyle\doteq
. Environments have no special
\displaystyle\square
form. However, application and record projection must accommodate the case where the selection on the closure or record being eliminated is represented by
\displaystyle\square
. In these rules
\displaystyle\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}\doteq
is used to denote the relational composition of
\displaystyle\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}
and
\displaystyle\doteq
.

Lemma 3.4 (Monotonicity of
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
).

Suppose
\displaystyle T::\bm{\rho},\bm{e}\Rightarrow\bm{v}
with
\displaystyle\rho,e,\alpha\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}v
and
\displaystyle\rho^{\prime},e^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}v^{\prime}
. If
\displaystyle(\rho,e,\alpha)\sqsubseteq(\rho^{\prime},e^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime})
then
\displaystyle v\sqsubseteq v^{\prime}
.

3.3.
Backward data dependency

The backward dependency function
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
‘‘rewinds’’ evaluation, turning output demand into input demand, with
\displaystyle T
guiding the analysis backward. We start with the auxiliary function
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}w}}}
which is used for backward-analysing a pattern-match.

10
defines a family of

functions

\displaystyle w

\displaystyle\alpha

\displaystyle\bm{v}

Figure 10
.
Backward data dependency (Boolean cases for
\displaystyle\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}
omitted)

In the variable case, no proper part of
\displaystyle\bm{v}
was matched, so
\displaystyle\alpha
is disregarded. The rule need only ensure that the demand
\displaystyle v
in the singleton environment
\displaystyle x{:}\;v
is propagated backward. If a Boolean constant was matched,
\displaystyle\alpha
becomes the demand on that constant, and
\displaystyle\kappa
, capturing the demand on the continuation, is used to construct the demand on the original eliminator, with
\displaystyle\square
used to represent the absence of demand on the non-taken branch. (Using
\displaystyle\square
for this means matches
\displaystyle w
need only retain information about taken branches.) The nil case is similar.

For a cons match
\displaystyle{w}\,\textbf{{\text{{:}}}}\,{w^{\prime}}
, we split the environment into
\displaystyle\rho
and
\displaystyle\rho^{\prime}
(there is a unique well-typed decomposition) and then backward-match
\displaystyle w
and
\displaystyle w^{\prime}
recursively to obtain
\displaystyle v
and
\displaystyle v^{\prime}
, representing the demand on the head and tail of the list. These are combined into the demand on the entire list, using
\displaystyle\alpha
as the demand on the cons node itself.
\displaystyle\sigma
represents the demand on the interim eliminator used to match the tail, and
\displaystyle\tau
the demand on the eliminator used to match the head, which are then combined into a demand on the eliminator used to match the whole list, with
\displaystyle\square
again used to represent the absence of demand on the nil branch. Records are similar, except there is only a single branch, and the selection state
\displaystyle\beta
computed for the initial part of the record is an artefact of processing records recursively, and is disregarded.

Lemma 3.5 (Monotonicity of
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}w}}}
).

Suppose
\displaystyle w::\bm{v},\bm{\sigma}\rightsquigarrow\bm{\rho},\bm{\kappa}
, with
\displaystyle\rho,\kappa,\alpha\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}w}}v,\sigma
and
\displaystyle\rho^{\prime},\kappa^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}w}}v^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime}
. If
\displaystyle(\rho,\kappa,\alpha)\sqsubseteq(\rho^{\prime},\kappa^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime})
then
\displaystyle(v,\sigma)\sqsubseteq(v^{\prime},\sigma)
.

3.3.2.
Backward evaluation

Figure
10
also defines a family of
backward-evaluation
functions
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
of type
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho},\bm{e}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\times\mathcal{A}
for any
\displaystyle T::\bm{\rho},\bm{e}\Rightarrow\bm{v}
. Backward evaluation rewinds
\displaystyle T
, using the output selection
\displaystyle v\in\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
to determine an input selection
\displaystyle(\rho,e)\in\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho},\bm{e}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
. The rules resemble those of the evaluation relation
\displaystyle\Rightarrow
with inputs and outputs flipped, and with an additional output
\displaystyle\alpha
called the
ambient demand
. The general pattern is that each backward rule takes the join of the demand attached to any partial values constructed at that step, and the ambient demand associated with any subcomputations, and passes it upwards as the new ambient demand. The output environment is constructed similarly, by joining the demand flowing back through the environment copies used to evaluate subcomputations. Demand is also attached to the source expression when it is the expression form responsible for the construction of a demanded value.

Function application

The application rule is where the ambient demand is used and the function context changes, so we start here. The rule essentially runs the forward evaluation rule in reverse, using the trace
\displaystyle T^{\prime}
to backward-evaluate the function body. The ambient demand
\displaystyle\beta
associated with
\displaystyle T^{\prime}
is the join of the demand on any resources constructed directly by that function invocation, and is transferred to the matched part of the function argument by the backward-match function
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}w}}}
. The ambient demand passed upwards into the enclosing function context is
\displaystyle\alpha\sqcup\alpha^{\prime}
, representing the resources needed along
\displaystyle T
and
\displaystyle U
. The auxiliary function
\displaystyle\smash{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\rho,h}}}:\smash{\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho^{\prime}}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho},\bm{h}}\,{\mathcal{A}}}\times\mathcal{A}
for any
\displaystyle\bm{\rho},\bm{h}\twoheadrightarrow\bm{\rho^{\prime}}
defined at the bottom of Figure
10
is used to turn
\displaystyle\rho_{2}
, capturing the demand flowing back through any recursive uses of the function and any others with which it was mutually defined, into information that can be merged back into the demand on the closure. The function
\displaystyle\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\rho,h}}
is also used in the letrec rule, which otherwise follows the generic pattern described above.

Other rules

In the variable case, no partial values were constructed during evaluation and there are no subcomputations, so the ambient demand is
\displaystyle\bot
, the unit for
\displaystyle\sqcup
. The returned environment selection demands
\displaystyle v
for the variable
\displaystyle x
and
\displaystyle\square
for all other variables, using the family of
backwards lookup
functions
\displaystyle{-}\mathrel{\ni_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\rho}}}x{:}\;-
of type
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
for any
\displaystyle x{:}\;\bm{v}\in{\bm{\rho}}
also defined in Figure
10
. (The output of the function is on the left in the relational notation.) For atomic values such as integers and nil, the ambient demand is simply the demand
\displaystyle\alpha
associated with the constructed value, which is also attached to the corresponding expression, and the environment demand has
\displaystyle\square
for every variable in the original environment
\displaystyle\bm{\rho}
, written
\displaystyle\square_{\bm{\rho}}
.

For closures, the ambient demand is unpacked along with the other components, preserving any internal selections on
\displaystyle\rho
and
\displaystyle\sigma
. Composite values such as records and cons cells follow the general pattern; thus for records, the ambient demands
\displaystyle\alpha^{\prime}_{i}
for the subcomputations are joined with the
\displaystyle\alpha
on the record itself to produce the ambient demand passed upward. Record projection never demands the record constructor itself, but simply promotes the field demand into a record demand, using using
\displaystyle\mathrel{\ni_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\displaystyle\hfil\displaystyle x{:}\;\bm{v}\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\displaystyle\hfil\textstyle x{:}\;\bm{v}\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern Hole rule

The hole rule, as elsewhere, ensures that the function is defined when
\displaystyle v
is
\displaystyle\square
, and it is easy to show that
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
preserves
\displaystyle\sqsubseteq
, and thus
\displaystyle\doteq
.

Lemma 3.6 (Monotonicity of
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
).

Suppose
\displaystyle T::\bm{\rho},\bm{e}\Rightarrow\bm{v}
with
\displaystyle v\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}\rho,e,\alpha
and
\displaystyle v^{\prime}\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}\rho^{\prime},e^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}
. If
\displaystyle v\sqsubseteq v^{\prime}
then
\displaystyle(\rho,e,\alpha)\sqsubseteq(\rho^{\prime},e^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime})
.

3.4.
Round-tripping properties of
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
and
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}

We now establish more formally the round-tripping properties, alluded at the beginning of the section, that relate
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
to
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
. For the analyses to be coherent, we expect
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}({\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}(v))
to produce a value selection
\displaystyle v^{\prime}\sqsupseteq v
, and
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}({\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}(\rho,e))
to produce an input selection
\displaystyle(\rho^{\prime},e^{\prime})\sqsubseteq(\rho,e)
. Pairs of (monotonic) functions
\displaystyle f:X\to Y
and
\displaystyle g:Y\to X
that are related in this way are called
Galois connections
. Galois connections generalise isomorphisms:
\displaystyle f
and
\displaystyle g
are not quite mutual inverses, but are the nearest to an inverse each can get to the other. We will present a visual example of some of these round-tripping properties in §
4.2
; here we establish the relevant theorems.

Definition 3.7 (Galois connection).

Suppose
\displaystyle X
and
\displaystyle Y
are sets equipped with partial orders
\displaystyle\leq_{X}
and
\displaystyle\leq_{Y}
. Then monotonic functions
\displaystyle f:X\to Y
and
\displaystyle g:Y\to X
form a
Galois connection

\displaystyle(g,f):Y\to X
iff
\displaystyle f(g(y))\geq_{Y}y
and
\displaystyle g(f(x))\leq_{X}x
.

Galois connections are also adjoint functors between poset categories, with right and left adjoints
\displaystyle f
and
\displaystyle g
usually called the
upper
and
lower
adjoints, because
\displaystyle f
approximates an inverse of
\displaystyle g
from above, and
\displaystyle g
an inverse of
\displaystyle f
from below. Galois connections compose component-wise, so it is useful to think of them as having a type
\displaystyle X\to Y
, with the direction (by convention) given by the lower adjoint. If
\displaystyle f:X\to Y
is a Galois connection, we will write
\displaystyle{f}^{*}
and
\displaystyle{f}_{*}
for the lower and upper adjoints respectively; an important property we will return to is that
\displaystyle{f}^{*}
preserves joins and
\displaystyle{f}_{*}
preserves meets. We now show that
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
and
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
form a Galois connection
\displaystyle\mathrel{\Rightarrow_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
for any
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}
(Theorem
3.11
) by first establishing that the relevant auxiliary functions also form Galois connections.

Theorem 3.8 (Galois connection for pattern-matching).

Suppose
\displaystyle w::\bm{v},\bm{\sigma}\rightsquigarrow\bm{\rho},\bm{\kappa}
. Then
\displaystyle({\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}w}}},{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptw}}}):\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho},\bm{\kappa}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v},\bm{\sigma}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
is a Galois connection.

Proof.

See Appendix
B.2
. ∎

Lemma 3.9 (Galois connection for environment lookup).

Suppose
\displaystyle x{:}\;\bm{v}\in{\bm{\rho}}
. Then
\displaystyle({-}\mathrel{\ni_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\bm{\rho}}}}x{:}\;,{}\mathrel{\in_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\bm{\rho}}}}x{:}\;-):\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
is a Galois connection.

Proof.

See Appendix
B.3
. ∎

Theorem 3.10 (Galois connection for recursive bindings).

Suppose
\displaystyle\bm{\rho},\bm{h}\twoheadrightarrow\bm{\rho}^{\prime}
. Then
\displaystyle({\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\bm{\rho},\bm{h}}},\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998pt\bm{\rho},\bm{h}}}}):\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho}^{\prime}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho},\bm{h}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
is a Galois connection.

Proof.

See Appendix
B.4
. ∎

2.0mu\scriptstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\displaystyle\hfil\scriptstyle n\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\scriptscriptstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\displaystyle\hfil\scriptscriptstyle n\hfil$\crcr}}}}}}^{*})
provided for every primitive operation
\displaystyle\phi:{\text{{Int}}}^{i}\to{\text{{Int}}}
form a Galois connection of type
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}^{i}
. Under this assumption the following holds.

Theorem 3.11 (Galois connection for evaluation).

Suppose
\displaystyle T::\bm{\rho},\bm{e}\Rightarrow\bm{v}
. Then
\displaystyle({\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}},{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}):\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{\rho},\bm{e}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
is a Galois connection.

Proof.

See Appendix
B.5
. ∎

Establishing that
\displaystyle({\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}},{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}})
is an adjoint pair might seem rather weak as a correctess property: it merely ensures that the two analyses are related in a sensible way, not that they actually capture any useful information. This is a familiar problem from other approximate analyses like type systems and model checking, where properties like soundness or completeness are essential but do not by themselves guarantee utility. One could certainly define versions of
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
and
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
that are too coarse grained to be useful yet still satisfy Theorem
3.11
. However Galois connections do at least require that every tightening or tweak to the forward analysis is paired with a corresponding adjustment to the backward analysis, and vice-versa. In §
6
we consider how other ideas from provenance and program slicing might be adapted to provide additional correctness criteria.

4.
De Morgan dependencies for brushing and linking

§
3
addresses the first kind of question we motivated in the introduction (§
1.1
). In particular
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
can answer questions like: ‘‘what data is needed to compute this bar in a bar chart?’’, and indeed we were able to use our implementation to generate Figure
1
. The second problem we set ourselves was how to link selections between
cognate
outputs, i.e. outputs computed from the same data (§
1.2
). This is called ‘‘brushing and linking’’
(
Becker and
Cleveland 1987
)
in data visualisation, and has been extensive studied as an interaction paradigm, but with little emphasis on techniques for automation. Intuitively, the problem has a bidirectional flavour: one must consider how dependencies flow backward from a selection in one output to a selection
\displaystyle v
in the common data, and then forward from the selected data
\displaystyle v
to a corresponding selection in the other output. A natural question then is whether the analysis established in §
3
can supply the information required to support an automated solution.

An immediate problem is that the flavour of the forward dependency required here differs from that provided by the forward analysis
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
defined in §
3.2
. That was able to answer the question: what can we compute given only the data selected in
\displaystyle v
? But to identify the related data in another output, we must determine not what the input selection
\displaystyle v
is sufficient for, but what it is necessary for: those parts of the other output that depend on
\displaystyle v
. In fact the question can be formulated as a kind of dual: what would we
not
be able to compute if the data selected in
\displaystyle v
were
unavailable
?

4.1.
De Morgan duality

Why
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
is unsuitable as a forward dependency relation for linking cognate outputs can also be understood in terms of compositionality. Suppose
\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{1}
and
\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{2}
are the lattices of selections for two views computed from a shared input source, and
\displaystyle\mathcal{D}
is the lattice of selections for the shared input. Using the procedure given in §
3
, we can obtain two Galois connections
\displaystyle f:\mathcal{V}_{1}\to\mathcal{D}
and
\displaystyle g:\mathcal{V}_{2}\to\mathcal{D}
as shown in Figure
11(a)
below; we ask the reader to ignore Figure
11(b)
for the moment.

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{1}

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{2}

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{1}

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{2}

\displaystyle g

\displaystyle{g}_{*}
\displaystyle{g}^{*}
\displaystyle{f}_{*}

(a)

Non-composable Galois connections

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{1}

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{1}

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{2}

\displaystyle{f}^{*}

(b)

Composing via De Morgan duality

Figure 11
.
Dualising
\displaystyle g:\mathcal{V}_{2}\to\mathcal{D}
for composition with
\displaystyle f:\mathcal{V}_{1}\to\mathcal{D}

Unfortunately,
\displaystyle f
and
\displaystyle g
are not composable, as their types makes clear. While the upper adjoint
\displaystyle{g}_{*}:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{V}_{2}
has the correct type to compose with the lower adjoint
\displaystyle{f}^{*}:\mathcal{V}_{1}\to\mathcal{D}
, the result is not a Galois connection:
\displaystyle{g}_{*}
preserves meets, whereas
\displaystyle{f}^{*}
preserves joins. However, it turns out that if selections are closed under complement, we can derive an analysis of what is
necessary
for a given input selection from an analysis of what it is
sufficient
for. The effect is to invert
\displaystyle g
, yielding a Galois connection
\displaystyle{g}^{\circ}
with a type that allows it to compose with
\displaystyle f
. Then the composite
\displaystyle{g}^{\circ}\circ f
is a Galois connection linking
\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{1}
to
\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{2}
via
\displaystyle\mathcal{D}
, as shown in Figure
11(b)
, offering a general mechanism for brushing and linking, with nice round-tripping properties. We now unpack this in more detail.

First we shift settings from the lattices used in §
3
to Boolean lattices (or Boolean algebras)
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}=\langle\mathcal{A},\top,\bot,\sqcap,\sqcup,\neg\rangle
, which are lattices equipped with an involution
\displaystyle\neg:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
called
complement
. Boolean algebras satisfy complementation laws
\displaystyle x\sqcap\neg x=\bot
and
\displaystyle x\sqcup\neg x=\top
and De Morgan laws
\displaystyle\neg x\sqcap\neg y=\neg(x\sqcup y)
and
\displaystyle\neg x\sqcup\neg y=\neg(x\sqcap y)
. If
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}
is a Boolean algebra, then
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
is also a Boolean algebra, with the Boolean operations, and in particular
\displaystyle\neg_{\bm{v}}:\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{v}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
, defined pointwise. An additional distinguished selectable value
\displaystyle\blacksquare
serves as the negation of
\displaystyle\square
. The two-point lattice
\displaystyle 2
we used to illustrate §
3
is also a Boolean algebra
\displaystyle\langle 2,\mathsf{tt},\mathsf{ff},\wedge,\vee,\neg\rangle
with
\displaystyle\neg
corresponding to logical negation.

Matrix convolution example, with methods
