for dealing with boundaries

It is an easy consequence of the complementation and De Morgan laws that any meet-preserving operation
\displaystyle g:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
on Boolean algebras has a join-preserving De Morgan dual
\displaystyle{g}^{\circ}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
given by
\displaystyle\neg_{\mathcal{B}}\circ g\circ\neg_{\mathcal{A}}
, and any join-preserving operation
\displaystyle h
has a meet-preserving De Morgan dual
\displaystyle{h}^{\circ}
defined similarly. Moreover if
\displaystyle h
is the lower adjoint of
\displaystyle g
, then
\displaystyle{g}^{\circ}
is the lower adjoint of
\displaystyle{h}^{\circ}
. Thus Galois connections on Boolean algebras also admit a (contravariant) notion of De Morgan duality, defined component-wise.

Definition 4.1 (De Morgan dual of a Galois connection).

Suppose
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}
and
\displaystyle\mathcal{B}
are Boolean algebras and
\displaystyle f:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
is a Galois connection
\displaystyle({f}^{*},{f}_{*})
. Define the
De Morgan dual

\displaystyle{f}^{\circ}
of
\displaystyle f
to be the Galois connection
\displaystyle({{f}_{*}}^{\circ},{{f}^{*}}^{\circ}):\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{A}
.

Dualising a Galois connection flips the direction of the arrow by swapping the roles of the upper and lower adjoints. So while
\displaystyle f:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
and
\displaystyle g:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}
are not composable,
\displaystyle f
and
\displaystyle{g}^{\circ}:\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
are, and the composition is achieved by transforming
\displaystyle{g}_{*}
from something which determines what we can compute with
\displaystyle v
into something which determines what we cannot compute without
\displaystyle v
. This offers a principled basis for an automated brushing and linking feature between cognate computations
\displaystyle T
and
\displaystyle U
. When the user selects part of the output of
\displaystyle T
, we can use
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
to compute the needed data
\displaystyle v
, and then use
\displaystyle{{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptU}}}}^{\circ}
to compute the parts of the output of
\displaystyle U
that depend on
\displaystyle v
. This is the approach implemented in Fluid, and we used this to generate Figure
2
in §
1.2
.

4.2.
Example: matrix convolution

We now illustrate the
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\Rightarrow_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}}^{\circ}
Galois connection, contrasting it with
\displaystyle\mathrel{\Rightarrow_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
, using an example which computes the convolution of a
\displaystyle 5\times 5
matrix with a
\displaystyle 3\times 3
kernel. Convolution has an intuitive dependency structure and the values involved have an easy visual presentation, making it useful for conveying the flavour of the four distinct (but connected) dependency relations that arise in the framework. The source code for the example is given in Figure
12
, and shows the
convolve
function, plus
zero
,
wrap
and
extend
which provide different methods for handling the boundaries of the input matrix. The angle-bracket notation is used to construct matrices, which were omitted from §
2
. (The formal treatment is similar to records.)

(a)

Galois dependency
\displaystyle\mathrel{\Rightarrow_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}

(b)

De Morgan dual
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\Rightarrow_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}}^{\circ}

Figure 13
.
Upper and lower pairs are dual; left and right pairs are adjoint

Fluid was used to generate the diagrams in Figure
13
, which show the four dependency relations and two of their four possible round-trips. Figure
13(a)
shows the
\displaystyle\mathrel{\Rightarrow_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
Galois connection defined in §
3.4
. In the upper figure, the user selects (in green) the output cell at position
\displaystyle(2,2)
(counting rows downwards from
\displaystyle 1
). This induces a demand (via the lower adjoint
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
) on the input matrix
image
and the kernel
filter
, revealing (in yellow) that the entire kernel was needed to compute the value
\displaystyle 1
, but only some of the input matrix. In particular the elements at
\displaystyle(1,3)
and
\displaystyle(3,1)
in
image
were not needed, because of zeros present in
filter
. If we then ‘‘round-trip’’ that input selection, computing the corresponding availability on the output using the upper adjoint
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
, the green selection grows: it turns out that the data needed to make
\displaystyle(2,2)
available are sufficient to make
\displaystyle(1,1)
available as well.

Figure
13(b)
shows the De Morgan dual
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\Rightarrow_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}}^{\circ}
. In the upper part of the figure, the user selects (green) kernel cell
\displaystyle(1,2)
to see the output cells that depend on it. This is computed using the De Morgan dual of
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
. First we negate the input selection, marking
\displaystyle(1,2)
as unavailable, and all other inputs as available. Then we forward-analyse with
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
to determine that with this data selection, we can only compute the top row of the output. (If it seems odd that we can compute even the top row, notice that the example uses the method
zero
for dealing with boundaries;
wrap
or
extend
would give a different behaviour.) Then we negate that top row selection to produce the (yellow) output selection shown in the figure. These are exactly the output cells which depend on kernel cell (
\displaystyle 1,2)
in the sense that they cannot be computed if that input is unavailable.

We can then round-trip this output selection using the De Morgan dual of
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
. We first negate the yellow output selection (selecting the top row of the output again), and then use
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
to determine the needed inputs, which turn out to be the top two rows of
image
, and the top row of
filter
. Negating again produces the green output selection shown in the lower figure. Thus the backwards De Morgan dual computes the inputs that would
not
be needed if the selected outputs were not needed: more economically, the inputs that are
only
needed for the selected output. Here the round-trip reveals that if kernel cell
\displaystyle(1,2)
is unavailable, then the entire top row of the kernel might as well have been unavailable too, and similarly for the bottom 3 rows of the input.

Figure 14
.
Differential Galois slicing selects input (yellow) needed
only
for selected output (green)

The De Morgan dual puts us in a better position to consider the relationship between the present system and earlier work on
Galois slicing
, a program slicing technique that has been explored for pure functional programs
(
Perera
et al. 2012
)
, functional programs with effects
(
Ricciotti et al. 2017
)
, and
\displaystyle\pi
-calculus
(
Perera
et al. 2016
)
. We consider other related work in §
6.1
.

Galois slicing operates on lattices of
slices
, which are programs (or values) where parts deemed irrelevant are replaced by a hole
\displaystyle\square
. (If we think of the notion of selection defined in §
3.1.1
as picking out a subset of the paths in a term, then slices resembles selections which are prefix-closed, meaning that if a given path in a term is selected, then so are all of its prefixes.) For a fixed computation, a meet-preserving
forward-slicing
function is defined which takes input slices to output slices, discarding parts which cannot be computed because the needed input is not present, plus a join-preserving
backward-slicing
function taking output slices to input slices, retaining the parts needed for the output slice. For example Figure
14(a)
shows a computation with output
(0.4,

0.6)
, and Figure
14(b)
gives the backward slice for output slice
(0.4,
\displaystyle\square
)
. Forward and backward slicing, for a given computation, form a Galois connection, giving the analyses the nice round-tripping properties we motivated in §
3.4
.

Unfortunately, the notion of slice does not lend itself to computing dependencies where the needed input or output is a proper part of a value, such as a component of a tuple.
Differential
slicing
(
Perera
et al. 2012
)
improves on this by using Galois slicing to compute a pair of input slices
\displaystyle(e,e^{\prime}
) for a pair of output slices
\displaystyle(v,v^{\prime})
where
\displaystyle v\sqsubseteq v^{\prime}
. By monotonicity,
\displaystyle e\sqsubseteq e^{\prime}
. This can be used to compute a (differential) slice for an arbitrary subtree, by setting
\displaystyle v
to be the ‘‘spine’’ of the original output up to the location of the subtree, and
\displaystyle v^{\prime}
to be
\displaystyle v
with the subtree of interest plugged back in. Here we could focus on the value
0.4
in the output by computing the backward slice for
(
\displaystyle\square
,
\displaystyle\square
)
(Figure
14(c)
) and then comparing it with the backward slice for
(0.4,
\displaystyle\square
)
, generating a differential slice where the parts that are different are highlighted (Figure
14(d)
). But although it supports a notion of selection which is closer to what we need, the differential slice highlights only the program parts that are needed
exclusively
by the selected output. Here,
2
and
3
are needed to compute the spine as well (in order to decide which conditional branch to execute), so they are excluded from the differential slice. In fact differential slicing is similar to the dual of
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
, and as such underapproximates the dependency information needed for data linking.

5.
Galois connections for desugaring

Elaborating a richer surface language into a simpler core is a common pattern with well known benefits. It can, however, make it harder to express certain information to the programmer in terms of the surface language. We face this problem with the analysis in §
3
, which links outputs not only to inputs, but also to expressions responsible for introducing data. We could use this information in an IDE to link structured outputs to relevant code fragments, but only if we are able to map term selections back to the surface program. We now sketch a bidirectional desugaring procedure which addresses this, and which composes with the Galois dependency analysis defined in §
3
.

5.1.
Surface language syntax

The surface language Fluid extends the core syntax with list notation
\displaystyle{\text{{[}}}s\textbf{{\text{{,}}}}...\textbf{{\text{{,}}}}s^{\prime}{\text{{]}}}
, Haskell 98-style list comprehensions
(
Jones 2003
)
, list enumerations, first-class primitives and piecewise function definitions and pattern-matching, as shown in Figure
15
. Typing rules are given in Appendix
A
, Figures
18
and
19
. We attach selection states
\displaystyle\alpha
to (selectable) surface terms
\displaystyle s,t
that desugar to selectable core terms, and let
\displaystyle\bm{s}
,
\displaystyle\bm{t}
range over ‘‘raw’’ surface terms, which are isomorphic to the selectable terms where the type of selection states is the unit lattice
\displaystyle 1
.

Figure
16
shows how the end-to-end mapping would appear to a user. (For illustrative purposes the library function
map
and some raw data are included in the same source file.) On the left, the user selects a cons cell (green) in the output; by backwards evaluating and then backwards desugaring, we are able to highlight the list comprehension, the cons in the second clause of
map
, and both occurrences of the constant
"Hydro"
. These last two are highlighted because the selected cons cell was constructed by eliminating a Boolean that was in turn constructed by the primitive
==
operator, which consumed the two strings. The user might then conjecture that the two occurrences of
"Geo"
were somehow responsible for the inclusion of the third cons cell in the output; they can confirm this by making the green selection on the right. (Highlighting
==
too would clearly be helpful here; we discuss this possibility in §
6.1
.) The grey selection is included to contrast the cons highlighting with the data demanded by the list elements themselves, which is quite different.

5.2.
Forward desugaring

To define the forward evaluation function
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
in §
3.2
, we performed a regular evaluation using
\displaystyle\Rightarrow
to obtain a trace
\displaystyle T
, and then defined
\displaystyle{\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.97998ptT}}}
by recursion over
\displaystyle T
, with
\displaystyle T
guiding the analysis in the presence of
\displaystyle\square
. There are no holes in the surface language, so we can take a simpler approach, defining a single
forward desugaring
relation
\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}
, and then showing that for every raw surface term
\displaystyle\bm{t}\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}\bm{e}
, there is a monotonic function
\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.63702ptt}}:\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{t}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{e}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
, which is simply
\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}
domain-restricted to
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{t}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
. The full definition of
\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}
is given in Appendix
A
; Figure
17
gives a representative selection of the rules.

5.3.
Backward desugaring

The backwards analysis is then defined as a family of
backward desugaring
functions
\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\bm{t}}}:\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{e}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{t}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
for any
\displaystyle\bm{t}\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}\bm{e}
, with the raw surface term
\displaystyle\bm{t}
guiding the analysis backwards. (The role of
\displaystyle\bm{t}
in disambiguating the backwards rules should be clear if you consider that
\displaystyle e
typically matches multiple rules but only one for a given
\displaystyle\bm{t}
.) Figure
17
gives some representative rules; the full definition is given in Appendix
A
To reverse a desugaring step, we take the join of the demand on any parts of
\displaystyle e
which were constructed at this step, and use that as the demand on the parts of
\displaystyle s
which were consumed at this step, turning demand on the core term into (minimal) demand on the surface term. Thus the effect of the list comprehension rules and auxiliary judgements is to set the demand on the comprehension itself to be the join of the demand of all the syntax generated during the elaboration of the comprehension, using auxiliary judgments
\displaystyle\searrow_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}p}}
and
\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}p}}
(Appendix
A
, Figures
26
and
25
) to transfer demand from eliminators back onto the guards and generators.

5.4.
Round-tripping properties and compositionality

It is easy to verify that
\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.63702ptt}}
and
\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}t}}
are monotonic. Moreover they form an adjoint pair.

Theorem 5.1 (Galois connection for desugaring).

Suppose
\displaystyle t\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}e
. Then
\displaystyle{\twoheadrightarrow_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}t}}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\smash{\text{\tiny def}}}}{{=}}(\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}t}},\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.63702ptt}}):\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{e}}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{\bm{t}}\,{\mathcal{A}}
is a Galois connection.

Proof.

See Appendix
C.2
. ∎

The
\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\bm{t}}}
Galois connection readily composes with
\displaystyle\mathrel{\Rightarrow_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}}
to produce surface-language selections like the ones shown in Figure
16
. This is useful, although somewhat monolithic. In future work we will investigate techniques for backwards desugaring at arbitrary steps in the computation (perhaps by interleaving desugaring with execution), and presenting selections on intermediate values (such as lists) in the surface language, even though they were not obtained via desugaring.

6.
Conclusion

Our research was motived by the goal of making computational outputs which are automatically able to reveal how they relate to data in a fine-grained way. A casual reader who wants to understand or fact-check a chart, or a scientist evaluating another’s work, should be able to do so by interacting directly with an output. Recent work by
Walny et al. 2019
suggests that developers would also benefit from such a feature while implementing visualisations, for example to check whether a quantity is represented by diameter or area in a bubble chart
(
Walny et al. 2019
)
.

Galois connections provide an appealing setting for this problem because of their elegant round-tripping properties. However, existing dynamic analysis techniques based on Galois connections do not lend themselves to richly structured outputs like visualisations and matrices. We presented an approach that allows focusing on arbitrary substructures, which also means data selections can be inverted. This enables linking not just of outputs to data, but of outputs to other outputs, providing a mathematical basis for a widely used (but so far ad hoc) feature in data visualisation. We implemented our approach in Fluid, a realistic high-level functional programming language. Our implementation can be found at
https://github.com/explorable-viz/fluid
.

6.1.
Other related work and future directions

We close by considering some limitations and opportunities in the context of other related work. Galois slicing
(
Perera
et al. 2012
;
Ricciotti et al. 2017
;
Perera
et al. 2016
)
was considered in §
4.3
.

Executable slicing.
Executable slices
(
Hall 1995
)
are programs with some parts removed, but which are still executable. Our approach computes data selections, not executable slices, but such a notion has obvious relevance in data science, since ‘‘explaining’’ a part of a result should (arguably) entail being able to recompute it.
Expression provenance

(
Acar
et al. 2012
)
explains how primitive values are computed using only primitive operations; however, this still omits crucial information, and does not obviously generalise to structured outputs. Work on executable slicing in term rewriting
(
Field and Tip 1998
)
could perhaps be adapted to structured values in our setting.

Dynamic program analysis.
Dynamic analysis techniques like dataflow analysis
(
Chen and Poole 1988
;
Reps
et al. 1995
)
and taint tracking
(
Reps
et al. 1995
)
tend to focus on variables, rather than parts of structured values, and lack round-tripping properties; Galois dependencies have a clear advantage here. A limitation of dynamic techniques which is shared by our approach is that they can usually only reveal
that
certain dependencies arise, not
why
, which requires analysing path conditions
(
Hammer
et al. 2006
)
. In a data science setting this would clearly be valuable too, and it would be interesting to see if the benefits of the Galois framework can be extended to techniques for computing dynamic path conditions.

Brushing and linking.
Brushing and linking has been extensive studied in the data visualisation community
(
McDonald 1982
;
Becker and
Cleveland 1987
)
, but although
Roberts and
Wright 2006
argued it should be ubiquitous, no automated method of implementation has been proposed to date. Geospatial applications like GeoDa
(
Anselin
et al. 2006
)
hard-code view coordination features into specific views, and libraries like d3.js and Plotly support ad hoc linking mechanisms, with varying degrees of programmer effort required. No existing approach provides automation or round-tripping guarantees, or is able to provide data selections explaining why visual selections are linked.

Data provenance in data visualisation.
A recent vision paper by
Psallidas and Wu 2018
is the only work we are aware of that proposes that brushing and linking, and related view cooordination features like cross-filtering, can be understood in terms of data provenance. In a relational (query processing) setting, where the relevant notion of provenance is lineage, they propose backward-analysing to data, and then forward-analysing to another view (but again, without the round-tripping features of Galois connections). However, theirs is primarily a concept paper, proposing a research programme, rather than solving a specific problem.

theme within that grant, and by The Alan Turing Institute under EPSRC grant EP/N510129/1.

Totalise --- backward slicing

Appendix B

Proofs: Core language

B.1.
Conventions

The symbol
➪
indicates that a proof obligation is being discharged, and IH
stands for ‘‘inductive hypothesis’’. We make free use of the totality of the forward and backward slicing functions, and the fact that all term constructors preserve and reflect
\displaystyle\sqsubseteq
, for example that
\displaystyle{u}\,\textbf{{\text{{:}}}}\,{u^{\prime}}\sqsubseteq{v}\,\textbf{{\text{{:}}}}\,{v^{\prime}}
if and only if
\displaystyle u\sqsubseteq v
and
\displaystyle u^{\prime}\sqsubseteq v^{\prime}
.

B.3.
Lemma
3.9

If
\displaystyle{\rho}\mathrel{\ni_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\rho^{\prime}}}}{x{:}\;v}
then
\displaystyle x{:}\;v\in{\rho}
.

Proof.

By induction on the proof that
\displaystyle{\rho}\mathrel{\ni_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\rho^{\prime}}}}{x{:}\;v}
:

.

Case

\frac{}{{(\square_{\rho^{\prime}}\cdot x{:}\;v)}\mathrel{\ni_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\rho^{\prime}\cdot x{:}\;u}}}{x{:}\;v}}\hskip 9.24994pt\textsc{
lab={{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}{{$\displaystyle\ni$-head}}}}
}

➪

\frac{}{x{:}\;v\in{\square_{\rho^{\prime}}\cdot x{:}\;v}}\hskip 9.24994pt\textsc{
lab={{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}{{$\displaystyle\in$-head}}}}
}

.

Case

\frac{{\rho}\mathrel{\ni_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\rho^{\prime}}}}{x{:}\;v}}{{(\rho\cdot x^{\prime}{:}\;\square)}\mathrel{\ni_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\rho^{\prime}\cdot x^{\prime}{:}\;u}}}{x{:}\;v}}\hskip 9.24994pt\textsc{
lab={{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}{{$\displaystyle\ni$-tail}}}},
right={$\displaystyle x\neq x^{\prime}$}
}

\displaystyle\displaystyle x{:}\;v\in{\rho}

IH

➪

\frac{x{:}\;v\in{\rho}}{x{:}\;v\in{(\rho\cdot x^{\prime}{:}\;\square)}}\hskip 9.24994pt\textsc{
lab={{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}{{$\displaystyle\in$-tail}}}},
right={$\displaystyle x^{\prime}\neq x$}
}

\displaystyle\displaystyle(\ref{proof:env-get-put:lookup-ih})

∎

If
\displaystyle x{:}\;v\in{\rho}
then
\displaystyle\exists\rho^{\prime}
such that
\displaystyle{\rho^{\prime}}\mathrel{\ni_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\rho}}}{x{:}\;v}
and
\displaystyle\rho^{\prime}\sqsubseteq\rho
.

Proof.

By induction on the proof that
\displaystyle x{:}\;v\in{\rho}
.

.

Case

\frac{}{x{:}\;v\in{(\rho\cdot x{:}\;v)}}\hskip 9.24994pt\textsc{
lab={{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}{{$\displaystyle\in$-head}}}}
}

➪

\frac{}{{(\square_{\bm{\rho}}\cdot x{:}\;v)}\mathrel{\ni_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\rho\cdot x{:}\;u}}}{x{:}\;v}}\hskip 9.24994pt\textsc{
lab={{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}{{$\displaystyle\ni$-head}}}}
}

\displaystyle\displaystyle\text{➪}\;(\square_{\bm{\rho}}\cdot x{:}\;v)\sqsubseteq(\rho\cdot x{:}\;v)

.

Case

\frac{x{:}\;v\in{\rho}}{x{:}\;v\in{(\rho\cdot x^{\prime}{:}\;u)}}\hskip 9.24994pt\textsc{
lab={{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}{{$\displaystyle\in$-tail}}}},
right={$\displaystyle x^{\prime}\neq x$}
}

\displaystyle\displaystyle\rho\sqsupseteq{\rho^{\prime}}\mathrel{\ni_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\rho}}}{x{:}\;v}\hskip 9.24994pt(\exists\rho^{\prime})

(IH)

➪

\frac{{\rho^{\prime}}\mathrel{\ni_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\rho}}}{x{:}\;v}}{{(\rho^{\prime}\cdot x^{\prime}{:}\;\square)}\mathrel{\ni_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\rho\cdot x^{\prime}{:}\;u}}}{x{:}\;v}}\hskip 9.24994pt\textsc{
lab={{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}{{$\displaystyle\ni$-tail}}}},
right={$\displaystyle x^{\prime}\neq x$}
}

\displaystyle\displaystyle\text{➪}\;(\rho^{\prime}\cdot x^{\prime}{:}\;\square)\sqsubseteq(\rho\cdot x^{\prime}{:}\;u)

∎

\displaystyle\displaystyle\rho_{1}^{\prime}\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}\rho^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu},h^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu}\sqsubseteq\rho,h^{\prime}\hskip 9.24994pt(\exists\rho^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu},h^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu})

monotonicity

➪

\frac{v\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}T}}\rho^{\prime}\cdot\rho_{1}^{\prime},e^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu},\beta\hskip 9.24994pt\rho_{1}^{\prime}\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}\rho^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu},h^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu}}{v\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}{\text{{let}}}\;{h}\;{\text{{in}}}\;{T}}}\rho^{\prime}\sqcup\rho^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu},{\text{{let}}}\;{h^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu}}\;{\text{{in}}}\;{e^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu}},\beta}\hskip 9.24994pt\textsc{
lab={{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}{{$\displaystyle\mathrel{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\Rightarrow$}}$-let-rec}}}}
}

\displaystyle\displaystyle(\ref{proof:eval-bwd-after-fwd:let-rec-premise-one},\ref{proof:eval-bwd-after-fwd:let-rec-premise-two})

\displaystyle\displaystyle\text{➪}\;(\rho^{\prime}\sqcup\rho^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu},{\text{{let}}}\;{h^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu}}\;{\text{{in}}}\;{e^{\prime\mkern-2.6mu\prime\mkern-2.2mu}},\beta)\sqsubseteq(\rho,{\text{{let}}}\;{h^{\prime}}\;{\text{{in}}}\;{e^{\prime}},\alpha)

∎

Auxiliary lemmas

Definition C.1.

Suppose
\displaystyle r\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}e
. Define
\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.63702ptr}}:\textup{{Sel}}_{r}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{e}\,{\mathcal{A}}
and
\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}r}}:\textup{{Sel}}_{e}\,{\mathcal{A}}\to\textup{{Sel}}_{r}\,{\mathcal{A}}
to be
\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}
domain-restricted to
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{r}\,{\mathcal{A}}
and
\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}r}}
domain-restricted to
\displaystyle\textup{{Sel}}_{e}\,{\mathcal{A}}
respectively.

Suppose
\displaystyle r\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}e
. Then:

and
\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}r}}
are monotonic.

\displaystyle\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\hskip-0.63702ptr}}(\mathrel{{\rotatebox[origin]{-45.0}{$\displaystyle\twoheadrightarrow$}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}r}}(e^{\prime}))\sqsupseteq e^{\prime}
